Outlines a comprehensive evaluation process, including red-teaming for risk assessment, to identify and mitigate potential model risks, particularly for emerging "frontier" AI models. 

Promotes transparency through model reporting and information sharing, using tools like model cards and data sheets to document AI systems. 

Engages in post-deployment monitoring and employs a bug bounty program to address vulnerabilities and misuse of AI models. 

Implements robust security measures to protect AI models, including a Secure AI Framework and engagement with external security experts. 

Explores technical solutions like watermarking and metadata to identify AI-generated content's provenance. 

Prioritizes research on societal, safety, and security risks, supporting external AI impact research through initiatives like the Digital Futures Project.

name: Guidance on Application of the Fair Housing Act to the Advertising of Housing, Credit, and Other Real Estate-Related Transactions through Digital Platforms
authority: Department of Housing and Urban Development
summary:
Explains how the Fair Housing Act applies to housing-related advertising via AI and algorithmic systems on digital platforms.

Prohibits discriminatory advertising practices based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability.

Warns that audience categorization and algorithmic delivery tools can unintentionally lead to discrimination by excluding or targeting groups based on protected characteristics.

Requires advertisers and platforms to avoid using AI tools that segment audiences by protected characteristics or proxies like geographic location.

Urges ad platforms to disable certain targeting functions for housing ads and conduct regular audits to ensure compliance with the Act.

Recommends that advertisers and platforms manage discriminatory risks by utilizing separate processes for housing-related ads and monitoring ad delivery outcomes for bias.

Advises documenting and publicly sharing information on ad targeting functions to ensure transparency and accountability.

name: Increasing AI Capacity Across the Federal Government: AI Talent Surge Progress and Recommendations
summary:
Mandates Federal agencies strengthen AI safety, security, privacy, equity, civil rights, and innovation through Executive Order 14110, signed by President Biden.

Launches a National AI Talent Surge to recruit AI professionals into the Federal Government, enhancing AI regulatory and policy capacity, government use of AI, and AI R&D ecosystem.

Facilitates AI hiring with Direct Hire Authority and Excepted Service Appointments granted by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM).

Establishes Chief AI Officers and enhances AI competencies with training programs for the Federal workforce.

Recommends funding increases for AI talent, institutionalizing tech talent programs, improving USAJOBS, and piloting skills-based hiring.

Proposes an AI scholarship-for-service program and public service cultivation within the tech ecosystem.

Encourages global AI talent engagement and provides guidance for improving Federal hiring experiences.

name:
Government-wide Hiring Authorities for Advancing Federal Government
Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
summary:
Mandates the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to conduct an evidence-based review for hiring and workplace flexibility for AI and data-science roles within 60 days of the Executive Order (EO) 14110.

Authorizes government-wide direct hire authority for specific AI-related positions, effective immediately through December 31, 2028, to address critical hiring needs in AI capabilities.

Permits use of excepted service Schedule A appointments for temporary staffing to support the implementation of EO 14110, with appointments valid for up to two years.

Requires agencies to submit quarterly reports detailing hires made under this direct hire authority, including job announcements and number of hires.

Stipulates agencies must adhere to veterans’ preference and public notice requirements when filling positions under these authorities.

Allows OPM to request information and assess the continued need for these authorities, with the possibility of modification or termination.

name: Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Consultation, Interim Response
summary:
Proposes strengthening existing laws and considering new legislation to address AI-related risks, particularly in high-risk settings.

Considers mandatory safety guardrails for AI systems in high-risk contexts, focusing on testing, transparency, and accountability.

Plans to work with industry to develop a voluntary AI Safety Standard and explore options for voluntary labelling and watermarking of AI-generated materials.

Emphasizes a risk-based regulatory framework to ensure proportionality and avoid unnecessary burdens on low-risk AI applications.

Commits to collaborating with international partners, aligning with global standards, and contributing to initiatives like the Bletchley Declaration on AI safety.

Supports investments in AI capability development and aims to maximize AI benefits, including through initiatives funded by the 2023–24 Budget.

Establishes an interim expert advisory group to explore AI guardrail options and harmonizes efforts with state and territory governments.

name: South Carolina Recommender System Act
summary:
Prohibits operators of internet-based applications, including social media platforms, from using automated decision-making (ADM) systems to suggest content for users under 18 who are residents of South Carolina.

Requires operators using ADM systems to suggest content for those 18 or older to either 1) Perform age verification of users through an independent third-party service or 2) Require users to upload government-issued identification, a current photograph, and personal information so age can be verified through publicly available records. 

Establishes civil penalties for violations of the above.

name: Rhode Island AI Commission Act
summary:
Establishes a permanent commission to monitor the use of AI in Rhode Island state government and recommend changes to the state’s use of automated decision-making (ADM) systems that may affect human welfare. 

Instructs the commission to continuously survey the state’s use of ADM systems, including identifying gaps in the procurement, evaluation, and ongoing testing of ADM systems, the training given to individuals using these systems, the transparency, explicability, and auditability of ADM systems, identifying and mitigating disparate outcomes due to protected characteristics, and addressing data security and intellectual property concerns. 

Requires the commission to include representatives from multiple state agencies (commerce, business regulation, children, youth, and families, etc.) and four from academic institutions. 

Requires the commission to submit an annual public report to the Governor and state legislature detailing its activities and findings, regulatory or legislative recommendations–specifically where state offices should or should not use automated decision systems, progress implementing previous recommendations, and the extent of algorithmic decision-making used by the state.

name: Automated Employment Decision Tools Amendment to NY Labor Law
summary:
Makes it unlawful for an employer in New York to use or implement an automated decision tool to filter employment candidates or prospective candidates for hire that has not undergone an disparate impact assessment annually.

Requires employers to provide the department with a summary of their most recent disparate impact analysis annually. Allows the Attorney General and Commissioner to initiate investigations and legal action if violations are suspected or found. Requires a summary of the most recent disparate impact analysis of the automated decision tool and the distribution date of the tool to be made publicly available on the website of the employer prior to implementing the tool.

name: Texas Workforce Commission Act
summary:
Requires the Texas House of Representatives committee overseeing workforce development to conduct a study on whether to establish a workforce training program, administered by the Texas Workforce Commission, to train individuals currently in the workforce in the use, operation, and creation of AI systems. 

Requires the committee to report the results of the study to the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Speaker of the House, and corresponding committee in the Senate no later than December 1, 2024.

name: An Act preventing a dystopian work environment.
summary:
Mandates that employers inform workers of data collection and distribution, including inputs for Automated Decision Systems (ADS), bans employers from collecting data for non-necessary business purposes, and mandates security measures to protect worker data.

Requires employers to inform workers before ADS use and annually provide workers with notice of all ADS in use, bans ADS use for employment decisions where there is potential for bias and/or discrimination, and requires third-party impact assessments to be conducted on such systems before and after use.

name: Illinois Public Act 103-0804
summary:
Amends the Illinois Human Rights Act to regulate the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in employment-related decisions.

Prohibits employers from using AI in recruitment, hiring, promotion, or other employment practices if it results in discrimination based on protected classes.

Requires employers to notify employees if AI is used in employment decisions.

Mandates the Illinois Department of Human Rights to adopt rules for implementing these AI-related provisions, including specifying conditions and timelines for providing notice.

Defines "artificial intelligence" as a machine-based system generating outputs like predictions or decisions that can influence environments.

Includes "generative artificial intelligence" as systems producing content simulating human-produced content based on prompts.

Takes effect on January 1, 2026.

name: Industries of the Future Act of 2020
summary:
Provides a multi-step plan in order to ensure that the United States will "continue to lead the world in developing emerging technologies".
Furthers the national interests and security goals of the nation.
Promotes collaboration between existing and new depraments.
Requires the Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy to submit a detailed report regarding current investments, research and development projects, and more regarding the US mission to be involved in the development of creating the industries of the future. 
Defines the industries specifically
Outlines a plan to increase funding and investments to developments in Artificial Intelligence and Quantum Information Science to 10 billion dollars a year by the year 2025.
Instructs the President to create a council called the Industries of the Future Coordination Council to support and guide the Director.
Outlines the membership guidelines and duties of the councils to uphold the objective that the US will lead the world in technology.
Specifies the termination date of the policy to be 6 years from enactment, on Jan 1, 2027.

name: 2023 UK AI Safety Summit Response (Microsoft)
summary:
Commits Microsoft to the responsible development and deployment of AI technologies, emphasizing collaboration with OpenAI and adherence to the National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework.

Establishes a joint Microsoft-OpenAI Deployment Safety Board for pre-release AI model review, focusing on safety and capability thresholds.

Implements multi-layered AI governance and continuous risk evaluation, including red teaming for security and misuse detection.

Advances transparency through documentation and stakeholder engagement, informing on AI system capabilities and limitations.

Invests in AI safety research and collaborates globally on best practices for AI governance.

Supports a coordinated licensing regime for frontier models to enhance oversight and risk management.

Introduces initiatives like watermarking and metadata-based provenance for identifying AI-generated content.

Provides a framework for vulnerability disclosure and mitigation, offering rewards through bug bounty programs.

name: Artificial Intelligence for California Research Act
summary:
Directs the California Department of Technology to develop and implement a research plan on the feasibility and risks of advanced technologies, specifically AI, to improve state and local government services.

Requires the research plan to include an analysis of the potential benefits and risks of using AI chatbots/assistance in various government benefit and welfare programs (such as disability insurance or affordable housing), a review of best practices from other governments, a cost-benefit analysis of implementing AI in government services, recommendations for effective integration (including risk management and monitoring and evaluation guidelines), and recommendations for mitigating privacy issues.

Instructs the Department of Technology to report its findings to the legislature before January 1, 2026.

name: New Jersey Bill A168
summary:
Requires the New Jersey Commissioner of Labor and Workforce Development to conduct a study on the impact of AI-powered technology and automation on the growth of the State’s economy. 

Requires the Commissioner to issue a report within a year that addresses the predicted impact of AI on the labor market for highly skilled professionals, the occupations most affected by and new professions that may be created due to expanded use of AI, the impact of AI on labor productivity and economic growth, and the implications for long-term workforce education.

name: Temporary AI Commission Act
summary:
Establishes a temporary New York state commission, composed of 13 members appointed by stakeholders in government and academia, to study the impact of and make determinations on how to regulate AI, robotics, and automation.

Requires the commission to study existing state laws and comparative state regulations for AI, the impact of AI on employment and data privacy, public sector AI applications, and the potential impact of AI regulation on industry. Requires the commission to make determinations regarding criminal and civil liability for AI-enabled violations of law and potential restrictions on AI use in weaponry. 

Requires the commission to issue a final report to the governor and other state leaders before December 31, 2024.

name: NY Office of Algorithmic Innovation Act
summary:
Establishes an Office of Algorithmic Innovation in New York to create policies and set standards that ensure algorithms are safe, effective, and ethical, and that the state is conducive to promoting algorithmic innovation. 

Provides the Office the power to set standards, audit, and establish statewide policy on algorithms used in technology.

name: Creation and Dissemination of Sexually Explicit Content Act
summary:
Proscibes disseminating "deepfake pornography" -- lifelike visual content that depicts sexual scenes which did not occur in reality, including images of nudity and sexual acts -- with the intent to harass, annoy, or alarm the depicted individual as a criminal misdemeanor offense in the state of Pennsylvania.

Exempts cases in which deepfake pornography was disseminated with the consent of the depicted individual from punishment under this law.

name: Synthetic Media Disclosure Act
summary:
Requires any person advertising property or services in New York to disclose when synthetic media is used in advertisements, including when synthetic media depicts a natural person, without the person’s consent.

Establishes civil penalties and fines if the above is violated.

name: New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan
summary:
The "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan" aims to establish China as a global leader in AI by 2030.

Promotes AI integration into economic and social sectors, enhancing national competitiveness and security.

Mandates the development of AI key technologies, including autonomous systems, knowledge computing, and intelligent robots.

Sets strategic objectives to achieve global AI leadership by 2020, 2025, and 2030, with specific economic targets and regulatory frameworks.

Emphasizes building AI innovation systems, fostering high-end AI industries, and upgrading industrial and social intelligentization.

Encourages military-civilian integration of AI technologies and development of AI-related infrastructure.

Establishes standards, regulations, and ethical guidelines to ensure safe, reliable AI development.

Supports talent cultivation and international cooperation to enhance AI R&D and application capabilities.

Outlines governance structures for implementing AI strategies and plans, including task monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.

name: California AI-ware Act
summary:
Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence in the California Department of Technology, which will guide state agencies' design, use, and deployment of automated systems in a manner that minimizes bias and promotes privacy and civil liberties.  

Requires state agencies to inform users they are interacting with an AI system, and provide instructions on how the user can reach a non-AI representative.

name: Massachusetts AI in Mental Health Act
summary:
Instructs licensed mental health professionals who wish to provide mental health services through AI to seek approval from a licensing board, inform patients of the use of AI in their treatment, provide non-AI alternatives, and obtain patient consent.

Requires any AI system used to provide mental health services to prioritize the safety and well-being of patients and be subject to continuous monitoring by a licensed mental health professional. 

Establishes disciplinary action by the relevant professional licensing board for mental health professionals who violate the provisions above.

name: New York AB A7859
summary:
Requires employers and employment agencies that use automated employment decision tools to inform job applicants:
(1) That such a tool is being used to screen candidates.
(2) Of which characteristics and qualifications the automated tool considers.
(3) Of what data is collected by the automated tool, where it is sourced, and how it is managed.

Defines "automated employment decision tool" as any computational process that produces an output which is used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making for employment decisions that impact natural persons.

name: Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Draft for Comment)
summary:
Requires AI-generated content in China to meet a series of criteria, including accuracy, non-discrimination with regard to an array of protected characteristics, intellectual property protection, exclusion of violent content or content that subverts state power, and respect for individual privacy.

Requires AI developers to conduct a security assessment on generative AI systems that evaluates the cybersecurity of the system and its ability to comply with regulations; the assessment must be submitted to regulators before the system can be released for public use. 

Requires AI developers to prevent their generative AI systems from being used for various purposes, including engaging in unfair economic competition, and requires generative AI systems to make themselves inaccessible to individuals who use the systems for such purposes. 

Describes the legal liability that developers hold for the content generated by their AI systems and the punishments, including fines, they may face for violating these rules.

name: National New Generation AI Standards System Construction Guide
summary:
Establishes a comprehensive framework for developing a national AI standards system, emphasizing the integration of ethical, security, and privacy standards.

Aims to clarify top-level design and develop key standards by 2023, focusing on data, algorithms, systems, and industry-specific applications.

Outlines an AI standards architecture, comprising eight categories: basic standards, supporting technologies, software/hardware platforms, general/niche technologies, products/services, industry applications, and security/ethics.

Emphasizes the need for international cooperation and alignment with global standards to ensure high-quality AI development.

Prioritizes the development of standards for key technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and quantum computing.

Addresses AI applications across various sectors, including healthcare, transportation, finance, and smart cities, ensuring cross-industry standardization.

Focuses on security and ethics, proposing standards for AI data, algorithms, models, and application security, alongside ethical guidelines for impactful AI use.

name: National Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Strategic Plan 2023 Update
summary:
Requires the federal government to coordinate and focus R&D investments in AI to ensure U.S. leadership in trustworthy AI systems. 

Reaffirms eight strategies and adds a ninth to emphasize international collaboration in AI research.

Prioritizes investments in fundamental and responsible AI research, human-AI collaboration, and understanding ethical, legal, and societal implications.

Advances safety and security standards for AI systems, ensuring they are reliable and secure from vulnerabilities.

Develops shared public datasets and environments for AI training and testing to democratize access to AI resources.

Establishes benchmarks and standards for evaluating AI systems, including fairness, privacy, and bias considerations.

Addresses workforce needs by training and retraining a diverse AI-ready workforce.

Expands public-private partnerships to accelerate AI advances and facilitate global collaborations for responsible AI development.

Emphasizes the importance of AI governance and the development of international guidelines and standards for AI systems.

name: AB-331 Automated decision tools
summary:
Defines an automated decision tool as any tool that uses artificial intelligence to make consequential decisions relating to employment, education, housing, utilities, healthcare and family planning, financial services, criminal justice, legal services, voting, or government benefits.

Bans the use of automated decision tools in ways that result in algorithmic discrimination on the basis of classes protected by state law. 

Requires any entity that develops or deploys an automated decision tool to perform an impact assessment on the tool, covering its purpose, outputs, use cases, inputted data, and potential discriminatory impacts, and the monitoring, safeguard measures, and testing conducted to mitigate adverse consequences. The impact assessment must be updated annually and after any significant update to the tool, and be provided to the state's Civil Rights Department. 

Requires any entity that deploys an automated decision tool to provide individuals affected by the tool's decisions with a notice that the tool was used and information on the tool's purpose. 

Grants all individuals subject to an automated decision tool's decisions the right to instead have those decisions be made by a human, if technically feasible. 

Requires automated decision tool developers to provide the tool's deployers with documentation of the tool's limitations, training data, and testing. 

Requires the developer or deployer of an automated decision tool to implement a program that governs the foreseeable risks of the tool's use, including designating an employee to monitor the tool and report concerns. 

Permits individuals and public attorneys to bring civil action against entities that violate this law, and makes violation of the law punishable by fines.

Exempts entities with fewer than 25 employees using automated decision tools that affect less than 1,000 people per year from some of this law's provisions.

name: Ethical Norms for the New Generation Artificial Intelligence
summary:
Outlines six general principles to guide ethical AI development in China, i.e. enhancing human well-being, fairness and justice, privacy and security, controllability, accountability, and improving ethical literacy.

Outlines 18 specific ethical requirements for AI development, which fall under categories of management and governance, R&D, supply, and usage.

name: TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management
summary:
Establishes a U.S.-EU Joint Roadmap to advance trustworthy AI and risk management, promoting shared democratic values and human rights.

Encourages risk-based approaches, aligning EU and U.S. methodologies, including the EU AI Act and the U.S. AI Bill of Rights.

Advances shared terminologies and taxonomies to foster interoperability and consistent application of AI risk management concepts.

Promotes leadership and cooperation in international technical standards, supporting transparency, inclusiveness, and innovation.

Develops a shared repository for metrics and methodologies to assess AI trustworthiness and risk management tools.

Analyzes existing tools to identify gaps and support AI standards development.

Implements mechanisms to monitor and measure existing and emerging AI risks, providing a tracker and interoperable tests.

Establishes expert working groups and consultation plans to advance short-term and long-term objectives in AI governance.

name: Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work")
summary:
Launch AI security standardization work by coordinating a system of AI security standards, focusing on foundational and application-specific research.

Accelerate development of AI security standards in key areas, driven by urgent needs and safety incidents, to address security risks and ethical issues.

Promote the application of AI security standards through pilot mechanisms and collaboration between academia, industry, and research institutions.

Strengthen training for AI security standardization talent by establishing multi-level training programs and fostering collaboration among universities, research institutes, and enterprises.

Participate actively in international AI security standardization by aligning Chinese efforts with global achievements, enhancing China's influence, and facilitating international cooperation.

Establish an early warning mechanism for high-security-risk AI technologies and products, including a catalog of risks and management standards.

Improve AI security supervision by developing an index evaluation system, enhancing AI supply chain security management, and formulating supportive standards.

name: Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Scholars' Draft)
summary:
Mandates the regulation of AI development and use activities within and outside China if they affect Chinese national interests.

Establishes principles of ethics, fairness, transparency, safety, and accountability in AI development and use.

Establishes aims and support measures for AI adoption, infrastructure development and supports data sharing, compute resources, and algorithmic innovation.

Protects intellectual property laws, user privacy rights and encourages applications of energy efficient AI products.

Implements a comprehensive oversight and coordination framework involving multiple government agencies. Mandate compliance with safety and security assessments, especially for critical AI systems.

Provides legal liability structures for violations, including administrative penalties, tort liability, and public interest litigation.

Promotes international cooperation in AI governance and allows for countermeasures against discriminatory foreign actions.

name: EU AI Act
summary:
Classifies AI systems into unacceptable, high, limited, and minimal risk categories, defining specific regulatory requirements for each category. Requires strict monitoring and quality management for high-risk systems. 

Establishes transparency and cooperation requirements for general-purpose AI models. Imposes additional risk management and evaluation obligations for general-purpose models with systemic risks.

Applies to AI developers and deployers whose systems are used in the EU market, regardless of their physical location, with certain exceptions.

Defines regulatory exemptions for free and open-source AI systems, subject to transparency and licensing requirements.

Establishes the European Commission’s AI Office to lead implementation efforts and enforce compliance. Allows significant penalties for violations. Defines additional AI regulatory roles for advisory boards and national-level authorities.

name: DoDD 3000.09 ("Autonomy in weapon systems")
summary:
Establishes Department of Defense policy on the development and use of autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons systems, including armed platforms that are remotely operated or operated by onboard personnel. Those policies include:

Requires  testing and evaluation requirements that must be met before a weapons system is deployed, including testing designed to ensure that weapons systems operate as intended even when subject to actions from adversaries. Outlines requirements that humans be able to intervene should weapons systems begin to operate in unintended ways. Establishes guidelines for the use of autonomous weapons systems designed to mitigate the probability and consequences of weapons systems acting in unintended ways.

name: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
summary:
Establishes legal framework for the use and governance of generative AI services in mainland China, promoting innovation while ensuring security and compliance with national values.

Applies to public generative AI services generating text, images, audio, video, but excludes non-public research and development.

Mandates adherence to laws, ethical standards, and the protection of intellectual property, personal information, and societal values.

Encourages independent innovation and international cooperation in AI technology, emphasizing lawful data handling and quality improvement.

Requires providers to ensure information security, sign service agreements with users, and prevent misuse by minors and illegal activities.

Obligates providers to label AI-generated content, maintain service stability, and establish complaint mechanisms.

Imposes oversight by relevant state departments, requiring security assessments for AI with social mobilization potential.

Specifies penalties for non-compliance, including warnings, service suspension, and legal action for serious violations.

Takes effect on August 15, 2023, with provisions for foreign investment compliance.

name: Global AI Governance Initiative
summary:
Calls on countries to enhance information exchange and technological cooperation for AI governance, focusing on security, reliability, and equity.

Opposes using AI for manipulating public opinion, spreading disinformation, or interfering in other nations' affairs.

Urges adherence to international laws and prevention of AI misuse by malicious actors.

Emphasizes global collaboration to make AI technologies open-source and accessible, resisting technological monopolies.

Promotes testing and assessment systems for AI based on risk levels, ensuring AI remains under human control.

Advocates for laws ensuring privacy and data security, opposing illegal data practices.

Stresses fairness and non-discrimination in AI development processes.

Calls for ethical principles and accountability mechanisms, addressing ethical concerns timely.

Encourages wide participation and consensus-based decision-making in AI governance.

Seeks increased representation of developing countries in global AI governance.

Supports UN discussions for an international AI governing institution.

name: Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office
summary:
Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to oversee AI advancements and enforce the forthcoming Regulation on AI.

Mandates the Office to develop tools and methodologies for evaluating general-purpose AI models, monitor AI market evolution, and investigate potential regulation infringements.

Requires collaboration with stakeholders, including the scientific community and AI developers, to advance best practices and codes of conduct.

Coordinates with national authorities and EU bodies to ensure uniform application and enforcement of AI regulations.

Supports international cooperation and the promotion of the EU's approach to trustworthy AI.

Tasks the Office with assisting the Commission in preparing relevant decisions and facilitating the uniform application of AI regulations.

Finances the Office through redeployment of resources from the Directorate-General and the Digital Europe Programme. 

Enters into force on 21 February 2024.

name: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Standardization 2021
summary:
Improve the working mechanism to promote AI standardization through the National Information Technology Standardization Technical Committee’s AI Technical Subcommittee.

Develop key AI standards based on principles such as “advantages first, maturity first,” focusing on performance benchmarks and hardware virtual interfaces.

Carry out pilot demonstrations to strengthen AI standardization promotion by selecting national innovation zones for standard application demonstrations.

Create de facto standards to enhance industry competitiveness by promoting AI standards through large-scale applications and integrating them into major projects and open-source communities.

Strengthen international exchanges by connecting with organizations like ISO/IEC JTC 1, participating in international AI standards formulation, and hosting AI-related conferences to promote Chinese contributions globally.

name: Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand)
summary:
Prohibits the use of GenAI for data classified as SENSITIVE or higher, and personal information should not be input into external GenAI tools.

Recommends agencies avoid using GenAI for business-critical information, systems, or public-facing channels due to risks of inaccuracy and bias.

Advises against using GenAI as Shadow IT, emphasizing the need for robust governance and accountability in AI application.

Encourages agencies to develop GenAI policies, ensuring ethical use, and promoting transparency and accountability.

Emphasizes the importance of considering privacy risks, recommending privacy impact assessments and engagement with Māori communities regarding Māori data.

Warns of security risks, including insecure code generation and data spills, advising strong cybersecurity practices.

Urges agencies to remain transparent about GenAI usage, ensure human oversight, and validate AI outputs for accuracy.

Suggests using sandboxes for testing GenAI safely and advises on procurement principles to mitigate vendor-related risks. 

This guidance serves as an interim measure while longer-term AI regulatory frameworks are developed.

name: Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance
summary:
Mandates embedding ethical requirements throughout scientific and technological activities, including AI, ensuring responsible innovation.

Requires adherence to rule of law in ethics governance, constructing a legal system for AI ethics.

Promotes agile governance for AI, dynamically adjusting to ethical challenges and risks.

Emphasizes the importance of openness and cooperation in global AI ethics governance.

Directs institutions to establish ethics committees for AI and sensitive areas, ensuring compliance with ethical standards.

Urges development of norms and guidelines for AI ethics, enhancing transparency and stakeholder participation.

Establishes the National Committee for Ethics in Science and Technology to guide AI ethics governance.

Mandates strict review and regulation of AI ethics, including risk assessment and compliance with international standards.

Calls for monitoring and early-warning systems for ethical risks in AI, ensuring rapid response to challenges.

Requires education and training on AI ethics for scientific personnel, raising awareness and ensuring adherence to ethical standards.

name: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions
Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act")
summary:
Regulates international and interprovincial trade in AI systems by establishing common requirements for design, development, and use.

Prohibits conduct related to AI systems that may cause serious harm to individuals or their interests.

Defines a "high-impact system" as an AI system meeting criteria established by regulations, requiring special assessments and risk mitigation measures.

Mandates responsible persons to assess AI systems, establish risk mitigation measures, and keep records, particularly for high-impact systems.

Requires publication of system descriptions and risk mitigation measures on publicly available websites for high-impact systems.

Obligates notification to the Minister if a high-impact system causes or likely causes material harm.

Empowers the Minister to order audits, require implementation of measures, and impose administrative penalties for non-compliance.

Prohibits possession or use of personal information for AI purposes if obtained unlawfully.

Imposes offenses for making AI systems available that cause harm or economic loss with severe penalties.

name: OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta)
summary:
Commits to continually evaluating and forecasting key areas of risk along several Tracked Risk Categories and indicating current pre- and post-mitigation risk in a Scorecard.

Commits to establishing safety baselines where only models with a post-mitigation score of "medium" or below can be deployed and only models with a post-mitigation score of "high" or below can be developed further.

Announces creation of a Safety Advisory Group to assist OpenAI leadership and Board of Directors with making safety decisions by overseeing risk assessments and handling emergency scenarios via fast-track process.

Tasks Preparedness team with conducting research, evaluations, and forecasting of risks, submitting regular reports to the Safety Advisory Group, coordinating with other OpenAI teams on recommended mitigations, and managing safety drills and third-party auditing.

name: The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper
summary:
Strengthens international security governance on artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies, and prevents and manages potential security risks.

Issues position papers on regulating military applications and strengthening ethical governance of AI.

Stands ready to strengthen communication and exchange with the international community on AI security governance.

Promotes the establishment of an international mechanism for AI governance with broad participation.

Develops governance frameworks, standards, and norms for AI based on extensive consensus.

Encourages responsible bioscience research and adherence to biosecurity guidelines.

Deepens international cooperation in information security, including data security initiatives.

Enhances studies on the impact of emerging technologies on global counter-terrorism efforts.

Calls for the formulation of global rules on digital governance that reflect all parties' interests.

name: Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence
summary:
Calls for countries to regulate military applications of AI to prevent strategic miscalculation and maintain global stability.

Urges countries to ensure military AI is not used to start wars or pursue dominance, respecting sovereignty and territorial security.

Emphasizes compliance with international humanitarian law, minimizing collateral damage, and preventing misuse of AI weapons.

Requires human control over AI weapon systems, ensuring data security, and restricting military use of AI data.

Recommends enhancing self-restraint in AI R&D, with accountability mechanisms and operator training.

Stresses the necessity of tiered regulation and risk management to prevent premature use of risky technologies.

Advocates for multilateral dialogue and cooperation to establish a universal governance regime for military AI.

Encourages developed countries to aid developing nations in governance capacity, opposing ideological divides and ensuring equitable technological advancement.

name: Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of AI
summary:
Calls for governments to prioritize AI ethics by establishing comprehensive rules, norms, and accountability mechanisms.

Emphasizes the need for AI ethical norms, laws, and policies to address potential risks and enhance AI security.

Urges governments to require R&D entities to integrate ethics throughout AI development, ensuring algorithm security, transparency, and data quality.

Prohibits the use of AI technologies that conflict with laws, regulations, and ethical standards; mandates quality monitoring and emergency measures for AI products.

Stresses safeguarding privacy and data security, advocating adherence to international norms for personal information handling.

Encourages public education on AI ethics and emphasizes the importance of public participation and awareness.

Promotes international cooperation to share AI benefits globally, participate in rule-making, and oppose exclusivity in technological development.

Advocates for international agreements on AI ethics, aiming to establish a widely accepted governance framework and standards respecting national practices.

name: Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics
summary:
Establishes a governmental policy framework for AI regulation, emphasizing sector-specific regulation and consistency with international approaches.

Adopts a risk-based approach and promotes incremental development and regulatory experimentation.

Encourages the use of "soft" regulatory tools and multistakeholder cooperation.

Recommends adopting ethical AI principles based on the OECD AI Principles, focusing on growth, human-centric AI, equality, transparency, reliability, and accountability.

Proposes the creation of an AI Policy Coordination Center to advise regulators, promote inter-agency coordination, and lead international representation.

Mandates mapping AI uses and associated challenges in regulated sectors.

Calls for the establishment of forums for regulators and public participation to ensure coordination and open discussions.

Urges active involvement in international forums to develop AI regulation and standards.

Advocates developing tools for responsible AI, including a risk management framework.

name: The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit
summary:
Affirms the need for AI to be developed and used safely, human-centrically, and responsibly.

Recognizes AI's transformative potential in public sectors like health and education while addressing risks such as disinformation and misuse.

Welcomes international cooperation to tackle AI risks, emphasizing transparency, fairness, accountability, and human rights protection.

Identifies particular risks with frontier AI, including potential catastrophic harm and manipulation of content.

Resolves to intensify cooperation on AI safety, especially regarding frontier AI, through international collaboration and future AI Safety Summits.

Encourages actors, including nations and companies, to ensure AI safety through testing and monitoring harmful capabilities.

Calls for building risk-based policies and enhancing AI capacity in developing countries.

Supports an international network of scientific research on AI safety and sustains a global dialogue to harness AI benefits responsibly.

Commits to further meetings and cooperation to address AI governance, involving countries like the US, EU, China, and others.

name: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Technical Documentation)
summary:
Specifies safety requirements for generative AI services in China, focusing on corpus safety, model safety, and safety measures.

Applies to service providers conducting safety assessments and the main oversight department for evaluating generative AI services' safety levels.

Mandates safety assessments and reporting, adherence to cybersecurity, data security, and personal information protection laws.

Requires corpus source safety management, verification, and traceability, including avoiding illegal content and ensuring intellectual property rights compliance.

Demands annotators follow strict training and rule adherence for data annotation and review.

Stipulates model safety, including foundation model registration, content safety monitoring, and ensuring generated content accuracy and reliability.

Outlines safety measures for service transparency, user data collection, and complaint handling.

Imposes rigorous safety assessment procedures and compliance for corpus, generated content, and question refusal rates.

name: Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the AI Industry in Shanghai Municipality
summary:
Promotes the high-quality development of the AI industry in the municipality by integrating AI with the economy, everyday life, and urban governance.

Defines AI as systems using computers to simulate and expand human intelligence and specifies the AI industry including software and hardware development and application.

Applies regulations to AI-related activities such as innovation, development, and governance within the municipality.

Mandates the Municipal People's Government to lead AI development and integrate AI plans into national economic plans.

Establishes a Municipal Artificial Intelligence Strategy Advisory Expert Committee for strategic advice on AI industry development.

Encourages innovation by citizens and organizations and explores a negative checklist for AI activities.

Supports international cooperation and participation in AI governance.

Encourages AI infrastructure development, including compute resources and big data centers.

Supports algorithm innovation and promotes the trading of algorithm models.

Strengthens AI talent cultivation and promotes AI technology standardization and intellectual property protection.

Implements regulatory measures for AI products, emphasizing ethics and security compliance.

name: Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority
summary:
Clarifies that 52 U.S.C. 30124 and 11 CFR 110.16 apply to fraudulent misrepresentation in federal election campaigns, regardless of the technology used, including AI.

Emphasizes that the statute is technology neutral and covers AI-assisted media, forged signatures, and other means of fraudulent activity.

States that the legal focus is on whether individuals fraudulently represent themselves as acting for a candidate or political party.

Announces that this interpretation will guide the Commission's future actions concerning evolving technologies.

Specifies that this interpretive rule does not require notice and comment procedures, nor does it bind the Commission or public.

Excludes the applicability of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, as the interpretive rule does not involve binding agency action.

name: National Security Memorandum on AI
summary:
Develop advanced AI computational infrastructure and adopt measures to attract top technical talent to work in the United States to ensure innovation and technological superiority in AI.

Instructs relevant agencies to protect AI intellectual property from foreign threats. 

Issue guidance on testing and evaluating frontier foundational AI systems to manage safety and security risks.

Directs national security institutions to harness AI to advance national security objectives through clear policies, strategies and coordination, while safeguarding human rights, civil liberties, and privacy.

Produce a strategy for the advancement of international AI governance norms in line with safe, secure, and trustworthy AI, and democratic values.

Requires covered agencies to appoint Chief AI Officer to managing risks and opportunities of AI

Requires the formation of an interagency National Security Coordination Group to harmonize polices related to AI in National Security

name: National Security Memorandum on AI: Governance and Risk Management Framework
summary:
Mandates agencies to identify prohibited and high-impact AI use cases, emphasizing risks to national security, human rights, and civil liberties. 

Restricts the use of AI whose output serves as the primary basis for decisions that could pose significant risks to human rights or national security, unless accompanied by human oversight.

Requires agencies to conduct risk assessments and implement minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI uses, ensuring human oversight and accountability.

Mandates annual inventories of high-impact AI use cases and establishes data management policies prioritizing AI systems.

Obligates agencies to appoint Chief AI Officers and establish AI Governance Boards to oversee AI activities and compliance. 

Stipulates standardized training for responsible AI use and development, ensuring accountability and documentation.

Allows waivers for certain risk management practices under strict conditions and oversight.

Ensures transparency and public trust through periodic reporting on AI oversight activities, with unclassified information made publicly available where possible.

name: Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (AI Content Disclosure)
summary:
Amends the title of statute 11.1303 to include synthetic media in political contexts.

Defines "synthetic media" as audio or video content substantially produced by generative AI.

Mandates disclosure in audio communications with synthetic media, stating "Contains content generated by AI" at the start and end.

Requires video communications with synthetic media to display readable notices throughout, indicating AI-generated content.

Authorizes the commission to implement rules, including possible exceptions to disclosure requirements.

Specifies that compliance does not exempt from other civil or criminal liabilities.

Establishes penalties up to $1,000 for intentional violations of disclosure requirements.

Exempts broadcasters from liability unless they are responsible committees.

Clarifies that the act does not alter the rights or obligations under 47 USC 230.

Applies disclosure requirements to communications created on or after the act's effective date.

name: West Virginia HB 5690 (AI Task Force)
summary:
Establishes the West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence within the Office of the Governor. 

Specifies membership including representatives from government, industry, education, and health sectors, appointed by various authorities. 

Charges the Task Force with responsibilities such as recommending AI definitions for legislation, identifying relevant state agencies for AI policy oversight, and developing best practices for public sector AI use. 

Mandates recommendations on AI's impact on employment, protecting individual rights and data, and addressing AI use in education. 

Requires the Task Force to assess current AI use in state agencies and consider extending its mandate to keep pace with AI advancements. 

Obligates submission of a comprehensive report by July 1, 2025, after which the Task Force terminates. 

Requires initial appointments within 90 days and quarterly meetings, with administrative support provided by the Office of Technology.

name: Michigan HB 2023-5144 (Election Law)
summary:
Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media produced by artificial intelligence within 90 days of an election if intended to harm a candidate's reputation or alter voting behavior.

Exempts media with a clear disclaimer that it has been manipulated and includes a citation to the original source.

Classifies violations as a misdemeanor for the first offense and a felony for subsequent offenses within five years.

Allows the attorney general, affected individuals, candidates, or voter organizations to seek permanent injunctive relief in certain courts.

Requires that injunctive relief complaints be non-frivolous and supported by clear and convincing evidence.

Defines "materially deceptive media" as AI-generated content that falsely depicts individuals in misleading ways.

Conditions the act's effectiveness on the enactment of House Bill No. 5143.

name: New Mexico HB 182 (Campaign Reporting Act)
summary:
Amends the Campaign Reporting Act to require disclaimers on advertisements containing materially deceptive media created through artificial intelligence (AI).

Defines "materially deceptive media" as content using AI to falsely depict individuals without consent.

Mandates disclaimers stating the content is AI-manipulated, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media within 90 days before an election if intended to mislead voters, unless accompanied by the required disclaimer.

Establishes penalties for violations: a misdemeanor for a first offense and a fourth-degree felony for subsequent offenses.

Allows enforcement and injunctive relief by the attorney general, district attorneys, affected individuals, candidates, or organizations representing voters' interests.

Excludes certain media types from disclaimer requirements and clarifies non-violation conditions for broadcasting stations and distribution platforms.

name: Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety)
summary:
Establishes a cause of action for the nonconsensual dissemination of deep fake sexual images in Minnesota, allowing plaintiffs to seek damages, including financial losses and mental anguish.

Defines the crime of using deep fake technology to influence elections, with penalties including imprisonment and fines for violations committed within 90 days before an election.

Criminalizes the intentional dissemination of deep fake images depicting intimate parts or sexual acts without consent, with increased penalties for aggravating factors such as intent to profit or harass.

Allows for injunctions and restraining orders to prevent further harm and includes confidentiality measures for plaintiffs.

Provides exemptions for lawful purposes, such as criminal investigations, reporting unlawful conduct, or scientific research, while ensuring compliance with federal law.

Specifies that these provisions are effective from August 1, 2023, and outlines jurisdiction and venue rules for related legal actions.

name: Michigan HB 5141 (Campaign Practices)
summary:
Amends campaign finance law to require that political advertisements generated substantially by artificial intelligence include a clear and conspicuous statement indicating AI involvement.

Mandates that AI-generated political advertisements in graphic form display the statement in large text, while audio communications must audibly disclose AI use at the beginning or end.

Requires video advertisements to display the statement for at least four seconds and include an audible disclosure.

Imposes fines for violations, with $250 for the first offense and up to $1,000 for subsequent offenses.

Exempts bona fide news coverage and platforms with clear policies on AI content disclosure from these requirements.

Defines "qualified political advertisement" as including various advertising formats related to elections or ballot questions using AI-generated content.

Conditions the act’s effectiveness on the enactment of House Bill No. 5143.

name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
summary:
Enacts the "Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act" to regulate synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Defines "synthetic media" as altered audio or video intended to mislead about real events or speech through advanced digital techniques.

Allows candidates misrepresented by synthetic media to seek injunctive relief and damages against the creators or distributors.

Requires disclosures on synthetic media: a visible text or audible notice stating the media is manipulated.

Places the burden on plaintiffs to prove synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Holds information content providers liable, not the medium, unless disclosures are altered or removed.

Encourages courts to resolve cases swiftly.

Declares provisions severable to maintain the act's enforceability if parts are invalidated.

Implements the act immediately upon passage due to an emergency declaration.

name: Utah HB 249 (Utah Legal Personhood Amendments)
summary:
Prohibits governmental entities in Utah from granting or recognizing legal personhood for artificial intelligence.

Restricts legal personhood to human beings and excludes inanimate objects, bodies of water, land, real property, atmospheric gases, astronomical objects, weather, plants, nonhuman animals, or any non-human taxonomic domain.

Applies these restrictions regardless of other legal provisions.

Enacts the bill with an effective date of May 1, 2024.

name: Alabama HB 172 (Use of Materially Deceptive Media in Elections)
summary:
Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media, produced by AI, within 90 days before an election if intended to harm a candidate's reputation or influence voting patterns.

Defines "materially deceptive media" as AI-generated content falsely depicting individuals in actions or speech they did not partake in.

Allows exceptions if disclaimers clearly state the media's manipulation and provide source citations for edited content.

Classifies violations as Class A misdemeanors, with repeat offenses within five years as Class D felonies.

Permits the Attorney General, depicted individuals, candidates, and voter-representing entities to seek permanent injunctive relief against violators.

Excludes distributors without knowledge of deception or intent to harm from violations, including media entities distributing content as part of legitimate news coverage.

Protects satire and parody, provided they don't rely on AI for impersonation.

Effective October 1, 2024.

name: Washington S 5838 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force)
summary:
Establishes a task force in Washington State to assess current AI uses and trends and recommend guidelines and potential legislation for AI systems.

Composes the task force of an executive committee with appointed members from legislative bodies, the attorney general's office, technology experts, industry representatives, and community advocates.

Charges the task force with examining AI development and use, focusing on safety, privacy, and civil rights, and submitting recommendations to the legislature.

Mandates a literature review on AI public policy issues, analysis of existing legal protections, and proposals for ethical AI guidelines and high-risk AI use identification.

Tasks the office of the attorney general with administering the task force, retaining consultants, and supporting subcommittee formation.

Requires the task force to deliver reports to the governor and legislature, with a final report due by July 1, 2026.

Expires the task force on June 30, 2027.

name: Oregon SB 1571 (AI in Campaign Ads)
summary:
Mandates that campaign communications using synthetic media include a disclosure stating the manipulation of images, audio, or video.

Allows the Secretary of State and the Attorney General to initiate legal proceedings to prevent violations of the requirement for disclosure in campaign communications using synthetic media.

Imposes a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for violations, with penalties directed to the State Treasury's General Fund.

Excludes certain media providers, broadcasters, and publications from the disclosure requirement, provided they acknowledge potential authenticity issues or involve satire or parody.

Adds the new provisions to Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 260 and amends ORS 260.345 to incorporate enforcement mechanisms for violations involving synthetic media in campaign communications.

Permits the Secretary of State to establish rules to implement these provisions.

Declares an emergency for immediate enactment to preserve public peace, health, and safety.

name: Utah SB 131 (Information Technology Act Amendments)
summary:
Enacts requirements for disclosure of synthetic media generated by AI in election-related communications, effective May 1, 2024. 

Mandates audio communications with synthetic audio to state, "Contains content generated by AI," at both the beginning and end. 

Requires visual communications with synthetic media to display phrases such as "This content generated by AI" throughout the video or image. 

Imposes a requirement for creators and sponsors to include tamper-evident digital content provenance in online advertisements, detailing the creators, edits, and AI usage.

Allows civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation.

Considers the intentional use of AI as an aggravating factor in criminal sentencing, effective July 1, 2024. 

Permits judges and parole boards to regard AI-assisted crime as an aggravating factor during sentencing. 

Maintains judicial discretion in sentencing decisions despite AI-related aggravating factors.

name: Florida SB 1680 (Advanced Technology)
summary:
Create the Government Technology Modernization Council within Florida's Department of Management Services to study and monitor new technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI).

Require the council to recommend legislative and administrative actions to promote data modernization and AI system deployment, and establish AI safety standards.

Mandate the council to assess AI's impact on legal rights and its use by governmental and private entities, focusing on potential exploitation by bad actors.

Direct the council to evaluate the need for digital literacy curricula and submit annual recommendations for government technology modernization.

Prohibit knowingly possessing, controlling, or intentionally viewing generated child pornography, with violations constituting a third-degree felony.

Forbid intentionally creating generated child pornography, imposing similar felony penalties.

Prohibit reproduction of generated child pornography in criminal proceedings, ensuring secure custody by law enforcement.

Specify the act's effective date as July 1, 2024.

name: Colorado HB 1468 (Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force)
summary:
Establishes the Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force in Colorado to propose recommendations for protecting consumers and workers from AI systems and automated decision systems.

Defines key terms, including "artificial intelligence system," "automated decision system," and "algorithmic discrimination."

Requires the task force to consider transparency, disclosure, and protection measures against algorithmic discrimination, and to recommend best practices for ethical and equitable AI usage.

Mandates the task force to include diverse representation and expertise in AI and related fields.

Obligates the task force to meet regularly, with an initial meeting by September 1, 2024, and to submit a report by February 1, 2025.

Permits the task force to continue meeting as needed until its repeal on September 1, 2027, subject to review.

Specifies that non-legislative task force members serve without compensation, but legislative members receive compensation.

name: Oregon HB 4153 (AI Task Force)
summary:
Establishes the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence in Oregon, comprising 14 members with diverse expertise.

Requires task force members to have proficiency in computer science, AI, technology industries, workforce development, or data privacy.

Mandates the task force to examine and define AI-related terms for potential legislation, aligning closely with federal definitions.

Requires the task force to gather input from a wide range of stakeholders, including academia, consumer groups, and businesses.

Directs the task force to report recommendations to an interim committee by December 1, 2024.

Provides that the Legislative Policy and Research Director offers staff support, and state agencies assist the task force.

Specifies that the task force ceases on January 1, 2025, with an emergency declared for the act's immediate implementation.

name: Connecticut SB 1103 (AI Automated Decision Making)
summary:
Mandates the Department of Administrative Services to inventory AI systems used by state agencies and make this information publicly available by December 31, 2023, with annual updates.

Requires ongoing assessments of AI systems to prevent unlawful discrimination or disparate impacts, starting February 1, 2024.

Directs the Office of Policy and Management to establish AI policies and procedures for state agencies by February 1, 2024, addressing procurement, implementation, and assessment to avoid discrimination.

Prohibits state agencies from implementing AI systems without impact assessments ensuring non-discrimination.

Establishes a similar framework for the Judicial Department, including inventories, policy development, and assessments.

Prohibits state contracts with businesses unless they comply with specified statutory provisions, effective October 1, 2023.

Creates a working group to recommend ethical AI use in government, assess federal AI guidelines, and propose an AI bill of rights for Connecticut, reporting findings by February 1, 2024.

name: Arizona SB 1359 (Deepfakes in Election Communications)
summary:
Prohibits the creation and distribution of deceptive and fraudulent deepfakes of election candidates within ninety days before an election unless there is a clear disclosure that the content is generated by artificial intelligence.

Exempts satire, parody, and interactive computer services from this prohibition.

Imposes a civil penalty for each day a deceptive deepfake is distributed without the required disclosure.

Defines a "creator" as a person using AI or digital technology to generate synthetic media, excluding technology providers.

Clarifies "deceptive and fraudulent deepfake" as synthetic media intended to mislead people about a candidate's actions or statements.

Defines "synthetic media" as digitally manipulated images, audio, or video to create realistic but false impressions.

name: New Hampshire HB 1688 (AI Use By State Agencies)
summary:
Prohibits state agencies from using AI to classify individuals based on behavior, socio-economic status, or personal characteristics if it results in unlawful discrimination.

Bans real-time and remote biometric identification systems for public surveillance, except by law enforcement with a warrant.

Forbids the use of deepfakes for deceptive or malicious purposes.

Mandates human review of AI-generated, irreversible recommendations or decisions before implementation.

Requires disclosure for content generated by generative AI if not reviewed by a human.

Informs users when interacting with AI systems.

Obligates state agencies to review AI use for compliance within nine months and align procedures with the chapter and ethics code.

Demands removal of prohibited AI systems and ensures new AI deployments comply with regulations.

Directs the Department of Information Technology to report annually on AI systems used by state agencies, noting compliance and changes.

Specifies the act's effective date as July 1, 2024.

name: South Dakota SB 79 (Child Pornography)
summary:
Defines "computer-generated child pornography" to include AI-generated depictions indistinguishable from actual minors engaged in prohibited sexual acts.

Criminalizes possession, distribution, and manufacture of child pornography, including AI-generated content, with varying felony classes and mandatory minimum sentences for first and subsequent offenses.

Prohibits defenses based on consent or mistaken age, but allows an affirmative defense if the depiction is solely of the person charged.

Mandates court assessments for convicted individuals and allows sentence mitigation in specific circumstances.

Requires prior out-of-state convictions for similar offenses to be considered in determining repeat offenses.

Specifies that certain materials with serious value are exempt from these prohibitions.

Incorporates offenses involving child pornography into the definitions of sex crimes, impacting registration and sentencing.

Addresses juvenile sexting, deeming it a misdemeanor if minors distribute or possess nude images or participate in prohibited acts using digital media.

name: Indiana HB 1133 (Digitally Altered Media in Elections)
summary:
Amends the Indiana Code to add regulations on the use of digitally altered media in elections.

Defines "campaign communication" to include media advocating for or against a candidate, with fabricated media depicting candidates requiring specific disclaimers.

Requires disclaimers for campaign communications containing fabricated media to state that elements have been digitally altered or artificially generated.

Mandates disclaimers in printed, audio, and video formats to meet specific visibility, audibility, and frequency standards.

Allows candidates depicted in fabricated media without the required disclaimer to sue the person who financed, sponsored, or disseminated the communication.

Entitles prevailing plaintiffs to recover actual damages, injunctive relief, and associated legal costs.

Places the burden of proof on the plaintiff to demonstrate depiction in fabricated media by clear and convincing evidence.

Expedites court hearings for related civil actions.

Declares an emergency for the immediate enactment of this regulation.

name: Maryland HB 622 (Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program)
summary:
Establishes the Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program in Maryland's Department of Commerce to support small and medium-sized manufacturers in implementing advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, to improve productivity and competitiveness.

Creates a special, nonlapsing Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Fund to provide financial support, with grants ranging from $25,000 to $500,000, requiring matching funds based on company size.

Reserves 20% of funds for manufacturers with 50 or fewer employees, allowing unused reserves to be reallocated to larger companies.

Requires grant recipients to report on fund usage within one year and mandates potential repayment if conditions are unmet.

Mandates the Governor to allocate $1,000,000 annually from 2024 to 2028 to the Fund.

Directs the Secretary to establish regulations for program implementation and commence the Act on October 1, 2023.

name: Hawaii SB 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii)
summary:
Mandates the University of Hawaii to establish a two-year program for developing a wildfire forecast system using artificial intelligence.

Requires the system to forecast wildfire risks statewide to enhance public safety and improve preparedness and risk mitigation measures.

Obligates the University of Hawaii to report on the program's effectiveness and provide findings, recommendations, and any proposed legislation to the legislature before the 2026 regular session.

Appropriates $1,000,000 from the state's general revenues for fiscal year 2024-2025 to fund the development of the wildfire forecast system.

Specifies that the Act will take effect on July 1, 2024.

name: Arizona HB 2394 (Digital Impersonation of Candidate for Public Office)
summary:
Amends Arizona Revised Statutes to prohibit digital impersonation using AI techniques.

Allows candidates or citizens to take legal action against digital impersonation within two years of awareness.

Mandates proof of unauthorized publication and lack of clear indication of impersonation to prevail in court.

Restricts legal action to originators of paid advertisements containing impersonations.

Exempts interactive computer service providers from liability for third-party content.

Permits filing for preliminary declaratory relief in superior court with expedited ruling requirements.

Specifies conditions for granting preliminary relief, such as immediate elections or significant harm.

Allows further injunctive relief and damages for impersonations involving sexual or criminal content.

Sets standards of proof as clear and convincing evidence for relief actions.

Defines "digital impersonation" as AI-manipulated media designed to deceive, excluding parody or artistic expression.

Operates as an emergency measure effective immediately to protect public peace and safety.

name: The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference
summary:
Urges extensive discussion on defining and scoping Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems (LAWS), focusing on autonomy levels, human involvement, and distinctions between civilian and military uses.

Advocates for LAWS to be governed by international humanitarian laws, highlighting uncertainties in distinction, proportionality, and accountability with current systems.

Supports developing a legally binding protocol on LAWS, akin to the Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons, to address legal gaps.

Warns that LAWS increase war's ease and frequency by lowering thresholds and costs, posing risks of indiscriminate harm to civilians.

Calls for caution in using LAWS, particularly to prevent indiscriminate civilian targeting.

Welcomes progress in LAWS discussions within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) framework and supports continued expert meetings.

name: New Hampshire HB 1432 (Deepfakes)
summary:
Prohibits the creation, distribution, or presentation of deepfakes intended to embarrass, harass, entrap, defame, extort, or harm reputations or finances, categorizing such acts as a class B felony.

Establishes an additional offense and liability for legal expenses if the deepfake results in an individual's arrest.

Exempts interactive services, media entities engaged in bona fide news reporting, election communications with appropriate disclaimers, and satire or parody from these prohibitions.

Allows individuals to sue those who knowingly create harmful deepfakes for damages.

Mandates that the secretary of state reject lobbyist registrations from entities convicted of deepfake-related offenses.

Specifies that provisions are severable, ensuring unaffected provisions remain enforceable if any part is invalidated.

Sets the act's effective date as January 1, 2025, following its approval on July 19, 2024.

name: Louisiana SB 6 (Unlawful Dissemination of AI Images)
summary:
Enacts R.S. 14:73.14 to criminalize the unlawful dissemination or sale of AI-generated images depicting nudity without authorization, with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate.

Defines the crime as involving images where the distributor knows they lack the authority to distribute or sell the images.

Exempts interactive computer services and providers of telecommunications or information services from liability if their systems are used for such acts by others.

Defines "another person" as someone whose recognizable image is used in creating AI-generated content meant to depict a real individual.

name: Delaware  H 333  (Artificial Intelligence Commission )
summary:
Establishes the Delaware Artificial Intelligence (AI) Commission to make legislative and executive recommendations on AI.

Mandates the development of statewide AI processes, principles, and guidelines for government agencies.

Encourages the use of AI in agencies to improve service delivery and ensures AI usage does not violate individual rights.

Requires an inventory of Generative AI use within state agencies to identify high-risk areas.

Comprises a 19-member commission, with appointments from state officials, academia, and the private sector.

Requires the commission to submit an annual report on activities, goals, and policy recommendations.

Places the commission within the Department of Technology and Information, with staffing support from the Chief Information Officer.

Sets an expiration of the Act 10 years after enactment unless extended by the General Assembly.

name: Tennessee Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council Act
summary:
Establishes the Tennessee Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council to guide AI awareness, education, and usage in state government.

Requires the council to submit an action plan to the governor for leveraging AI to improve government service efficiency and capture economic benefits.

Mandates the council to report annually on AI's impact on the labor market, propose legal and policy changes, and recommend workforce development strategies.

Directs the council to submit a final report by December 31, 2028, outlining AI governance frameworks, risk analyses, and recommendations for AI deployment in government.

Requires all state departments to cooperate with the council and allows the council to consult with AI experts.

Specifies that the council members will not receive compensation but will be reimbursed for travel expenses.

Repeals the act on December 31, 2028, and takes effect upon becoming law.

name: Mississippi S 3000 (Eight Universities Fund), Section 42
summary:
Reappropriates $53,478,000 from the Education Enhancement Fund for fiscal year 2023-2024 to Institutions of Higher Learning, maintaining original funding purposes.

Allocates $15,000,000 to the University of Mississippi for expenses in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, Healthcare Innovation, and related infrastructure.

Limits expenditure to the unexpended balance of funds as of June 30, 2023, and maintains the original purpose of the funds.

Allocates additional funds to Delta State University for flight simulators, Mississippi State University for computing infrastructure, and Alcorn State University for STEM programs, among other specified projects.

Ensures funds support technology transfer and entrepreneurial programs potentially linked to the Department of Defense and related federal research in Mississippi.

Requires consistency with the original authorization in Senate Bill 3002 from the 2022 Regular Session.

name: Virginia SB 487 (Use of Artificial Intelligence by Public Bodies)
summary:
Mandates the Joint Commission on Technology and Science (JCOTS) to conduct an analysis of artificial intelligence use by public bodies in Virginia.

Requires examination of policies for AI procurement, implementation, and assessment to prevent unlawful discrimination or disparate impact.

Requires public bodies to assess and continually review the impact of AI systems to avoid unlawful outcomes.

Mandates consideration of establishing a Commission on Artificial Intelligence to advise the General Assembly on AI-related issues.

Requires JCOTS to evaluate the composition and duties of this commission based on specified criteria.

Obligates JCOTS to report findings and recommendations to relevant House and Senate committees by December 1, 2024.
