name: Iowa S 2435 (Appropriations to the Education System), Division III, Section 6. ("GENERAL FUND APPROPRIATIONS")
summary:
Allocate $2.8 million to Iowa State University of Science and Technology to address workforce needs in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) by expanding degree and certificate programs in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, computer science, and related fields.

Promote innovation in areas such as digital agriculture, manufacturing, water quality, vaccine delivery technologies, and biosciences with the allocated funds.

Ensure that the state board of regents and the institutions of higher learning governed by them do not reduce budgeted funds for their police departments for the fiscal year 2024-2025.

Require the state board of regents to submit a quarterly financial report to the general assembly, including details on five-year graduation rates for the regents universities in the report for the quarter ending December 31, 2024.

name: New Hampshire HB 1596 (AI Usage in Political Advertising)
summary:
Prohibits the distribution of deepfake content created using artificial intelligence or generative AI within 90 days of an election if it involves candidates, election officials, or parties.

Exempts from the prohibition any media that includes a clear disclosure indicating manipulation by AI, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

Allows affected candidates or election officials to seek legal action for injunctive relief or damages.

Excludes liability for platforms providing content from third parties, individuals unaware of deepfake nature, and bona fide news reports questioning the authenticity of materials.

Excludes satire or parody content that doesn't rely on AI.

Requires disclosures to be easily readable or audible based on the media type.

Specifies the act takes effect on August 1, 2024, with severability of provisions if any are found invalid.

name: Hawaii SB 2687 (Deceptive Media)
summary:
Prohibits the reckless distribution of materially deceptive media, including deepfake and generative AI content, during election periods, to protect candidates' reputations and electoral prospects.

Establishes criminal penalties for violations, including petty misdemeanors, misdemeanors for repeat offenses, and class C felonies for intent to cause violence or harm.

Allows exceptions for broadcasters and online services that did not create the deceptive media, or if disclaimers indicate manipulation.

Mandates that disclaimers must be clearly visible and in the same language as the media, with specific requirements for video, image, and audio content.

Provides civil remedies for individuals or organizations harmed by deceptive media, including damages, attorney's fees, and injunctive relief.

Empowers the attorney general, campaign spending commission, and other authorities to enforce these provisions and seek injunctions.

Defines "artificial intelligence" and "materially deceptive media" for clarity and enforcement purposes.

name: Colorado HB 1147 (Candidate Election Deepfake Disclosures)
summary:
Prohibits the distribution of deepfakes concerning candidates for elective office without a clear disclosure, within 60 days before a primary or 90 days before a general election.

Requires a disclosure stating the content has been falsified if a deepfake is distributed.

Mandates that disclosures in visual and audio communications meet specific size and clarity standards.

Allows candidates affected by deepfakes to seek injunctive relief, damages, and other remedies against violators.

Exempts bona fide news, satire, and parody from the prohibition, as well as certain media and technology providers.

Obligates the Secretary of State to promulgate rules to enforce these provisions.

Permits civil penalties and administrative complaints for violations.

Establishes the act's effective date as July 1, 2024, with applicability to communications distributed thereafter.

name: Tennessee SB 1711 (Use of AI Technology by Students)
summary:
Mandates the board of trustees of the University of Tennessee, the board of regents, and local governing boards of state universities to adopt AI usage policies for students, faculty, and staff by July 1, 2025.

Encourages public higher education institutions to collaborate on policy development and implementation for AI use.

Requires these boards to post policies online and submit them to respective education committees by July 1, 2025, with noncompliance leading to mandatory reporting to the joint government operations committee.

Obliges the adoption of AI policies for students, teachers, and staff in schools by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reports due to the Department of Education starting July 1, 2024.

Instructs public charter schools to implement AI policies by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reporting to the Department of Education beginning July 1, 2024.

Takes effect immediately upon becoming law, citing public welfare.

name: Maryland  H 1128  (Talent Innovation Program and Fund )
summary:
Establishes the Talent Innovation Program in the Maryland Department of Labor to increase access to high-quality job training, with a focus on industries such as artificial intelligence.

Creates the Talent Innovation Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund to support the program, including job training and talent financing mechanisms.

Requires the program to conduct pilots, research, and stakeholder engagement to develop sustainable talent financing approaches.

Mandates an initial pilot program focused on the cybersecurity sector to expand regional cyber ranges for job training.

Authorizes the Department to provide grants and funding to various entities and individuals for training and support services.

Directs the State Treasurer to invest the fund's money, with interest earnings credited to the fund.

Compels the Department to adopt regulations and report annually on program activities and fund utilization to state leadership.

name: Washington SB 5152 (Synthetic Media)
summary:
Defines "synthetic media" as manipulated images, audio, or video that create a false impression of a real individual's appearance, speech, or conduct.

Allows candidates to seek injunctive relief or damages if their appearance, speech, or conduct is altered using synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Requires disclosure for synthetic media, stating, "This (image/video/audio) has been manipulated," with specific guidelines for visibility and audibility.

Places the burden of proof on plaintiffs to demonstrate synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Encourages courts to expedite proceedings related to synthetic media disputes.

Holds sponsors, but not mediums, liable unless mediums alter content or remove required disclosures.

Exempts interactive computer services from being treated as publishers of third-party content, except under specific conditions.

Mandates the public disclosure commission to adopt rules supporting this chapter without constituting violations under existing campaign finance laws.

name: Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2.
summary:
Create the Dyslexia Research Grant Program, administered by the State Department of Education, to support research on AI-based writing assistance for individuals with dyslexia.

Allow privately owned businesses in Nebraska researching AI writing tools for dyslexia to apply for grants, using a prescribed form.

Limit the total grant awards to $500,000, intended to be funded by the Education Future Fund.

Require all grant funds to be used specifically for researching AI tools that use aggregate writing analytics to help develop literacy plans for dyslexic students.

Mandate notification of the Attorney General if grant funds are misused, prompting a civil action to recover funds, which are then credited back to the Education Future Fund.

Authorize the State Board of Education to adopt rules and regulations to implement the program.

name: Idaho HB 2472 (Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act), Sec. 30
summary:
Amends the Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act to require utilization review programs using algorithmic automated processes to ensure that only clinical peers make adverse determinations based on medical necessity.

Mandates these programs to register with the Department of Insurance every two years and provide proof of compliance with Health Utilization Management Standards or equivalent standards.

Requires licensed physicians with relevant board certifications to establish criteria for these automated processes and verify their accuracy.

Obliges health care plans to have appeals procedures, allowing appeals to be filed orally or in writing, with decisions rendered within specified timeframes.

Ensures confidentiality of patient-specific information obtained during utilization reviews, restricting access to authorized individuals.

Permits adverse determination appeals to an external independent review, with potential further appeals to the Department if found arbitrary or capricious.

Authorizes the Department to issue corrective actions or cease and desist orders for non-compliance.

name: New York SB 1042 (Unlawful Dissemination of Intimate Images)
summary:
Amends the penal law to include the unlawful dissemination or publication of intimate images created or altered by digitization.

Defines "digitization" as altering an image realistically using other persons' images or computer-generated images.

Requires intent to cause harm to the emotional, financial, or physical welfare of another person for the offense to occur.

Mandates that the actor knew or should have known that the person depicted did not consent to the dissemination or publication.

Repeals subdivision 2-a of section 245.15 of the penal law.

Specifies that the act takes effect on the sixtieth day after becoming law.

name: New York SB 9678 (Materially Deceptive Media in Political Communications)
summary:
Amends the election law to require disclosure for political communications using materially deceptive media.

Mandates visual disclosures to be legibly printed, stating "This (image, video, or audio) has been manipulated."

Requires audio disclosures to be stated clearly at the beginning, end, and periodically for messages longer than two minutes.

Exempts satire, bona fide news reporting with clear disclosures, stations with consistent disclaimer requirements, and platforms disseminating third-party content in good faith.

Permits candidates depicted in deceptive media to seek legal relief, including court costs, attorney fees, and injunctions against unauthorized dissemination.

Grants courts authority to provide preliminary relief to plaintiffs likely to succeed in proving violations in upcoming elections.

Places the burden of proof on plaintiffs to establish use of deceptive media by clear and convincing evidence.

Clarifies that federal law takes precedence over state requirements for media labeling in political communications.

name: Bill limiting use of AI in elections
summary: Bans the use of artificial intelligence in the hardware or software used to (a) count, process, or adjudicate ballots, or (b) verify voters' affidavits, in Arizona.

name: UNGA Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development"
summary:
Resolves to bridge AI and digital divides globally and promote safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems to achieve Sustainable Development Goals.

Encourages Member States and stakeholders to support regulatory frameworks for responsible AI, fostering innovation and equitable access to benefits.

Calls for cooperation to assist developing countries in accessing AI benefits through capacity building, digital literacy, and infrastructure.

Emphasizes the protection of human rights throughout AI systems' life cycles and urges cessation of AI use that violates international human rights law.

Promotes inclusive governance of AI, addressing global challenges while considering developing countries' needs.

Recognizes data's importance in AI development and urges fair data governance to harness AI potential for sustainable development.

Encourages continued international cooperation, research, and mapping of AI impacts to inform effective governance.

Calls upon UN entities to assess AI challenges and assist developing countries in capacity building for achieving Sustainable Development Goals.

name: Stop Discrimination by Algorithms Act of 2023
summary:
Prohibits entities in Washington D.C. from determining eligibility for, or access to information about, "important life opportunities" (e.g., housing or employment) on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, familial status, source of income, or disability in a discriminatory manner.

Requires entities to provide a public notice describing any algorithmic tools they use to determine eligibility for, or access to information about, important life opportunities. The notice must be sent to any individual about whom such a determination is made.

Requires the notice described above to cover the data collected by algorithmic tools and how that data is shared externally, how that data informs the tool's decisions, and the rights provided under this act.

Requires entities to provide notice, to any individual against whom they take any adverse action (e.g., firing) on the basis of an algorithmic determination, that the individual may access and submit corrections to any personal information considered by the algorithm. A human must then redo the decision based on the corrected information.  

Requires entities to audit their algorithmic decision-making tools before deployment and annually thereafter to analyze discriminatory effects and other impacts, and then implement reasonable measures to address findings of unlawful disparate impact. Entities must submit a report on the audit to the DC government.

Permits affected individuals or the DC Attorney General to file a civil action in response to violations of this law, with fines up to $10,000 per violation.

name: Tennessee HB 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children)
summary:
Amends Tennessee Code to include computer-generated images created, adapted, or modified by artificial intelligence under the definition of materials related to the sexual exploitation of children.

Defines "artificial intelligence" as a machine-based system capable of making predictions, recommendations, or decisions, influencing environments, or learning autonomously, developed in any context, including software or hardware, and solving tasks requiring human-like abilities.

Includes "generative artificial intelligence" as a system capable of creating new content or data, such as text, images, audio, or video when prompted.

Takes effect on July 1, 2024, for the purpose of public welfare.

name: Illinois HB 4875 (Publicity Act)
summary:
Amends the Right of Publicity Act in Illinois to define "artificial intelligence" as systems that generate outputs influencing environments, including generative AI.

Defines "digital replica" as an electronic representation of an individual created using AI without their actual participation.

Prohibits the use of an individual's identity or digital replica for commercial purposes without consent during their lifetime and for 50 years posthumously.

Restricts the distribution of works containing unauthorized digital replicas without consent.

Exempts certain uses, such as in news, political campaigns, or works of public interest, unless they falsely create the impression of authenticity.

Incorporates elements from federal law to exempt certain service providers from liability if they act to remove unauthorized replicas upon gaining knowledge.

Applies to acts occurring after January 1, 2025, excluding ongoing or prior legal actions.

name: Utah SB 149, Chapter 70 (Artificial Intelligence Policy Act)
summary:
Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee the AI Learning Laboratory Program, which analyzes AI technologies' risks, benefits, and regulatory implications.

Mandates the creation of regulatory mitigation agreements, allowing participants to operate under modified regulations while testing AI technologies.

Sets eligibility requirements for regulatory mitigation, including technical expertise, financial resources, and risk management plans.

Requires participants to report consumer harm, privacy breaches, or unauthorized data usage, with potential removal from the program for violations.

Allows an initial 12-month regulatory mitigation period, with a possible 12-month extension.

Defines using generative AI to commit offenses as a punishable act.

Specifies the program's repeal on May 1, 2025.

Takes effect on May 1, 2024.

name: Utah SB 149, Section 13-2-12 (Impact of generative AI on liability for violation of consumer protection law)
summary:
Establishes that using generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a defense against violations of consumer protection laws.

Mandates disclosure when generative AI interacts with a person, requiring clear communication that the interaction is with AI, not a human.

Requires providers of regulated occupations to disclose when generative AI is used in service provision.

Prohibits service provision of regulated occupations via generative AI without meeting legal requirements.

Stipulates that disclosures be made verbally at the start of oral interactions and electronically before written exchanges.

Empowers the Division of Consumer Protection to enforce these provisions, including imposing fines up to $2,500 per violation.

Allows the division to seek court actions, which may result in injunctions, disgorgement of funds, or additional fines.

Permits civil penalties up to $5,000 for violating administrative or court orders, enforceable by the attorney general.

name: Utah S 84 (Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity), Part 13. Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program
summary:
Create the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program to award grants to business entities.

Require the development of AI courses and curricula for K-12 students, emphasizing practical training and career preparation.

Mandate business entities to partner with public or private schools when awarded grants.

Specify application requirements, including program details, school partnerships, and other collaborations.

Evaluate applications based on their potential to achieve program goals and overall viability.

Obligate business entities to enter a written agreement with the office detailing grant specifics before receiving funds.

Authorize the office to establish rules for application procedures, grant awarding, and post-award reporting.

Include an annual written update on the program in the report outlined in Section 63N-1a-306.

name: West Virginia H 3214 (Road Optimization Assessment Data Pilot Program)
summary:
Creates the "Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program" to study alternative methods for assessing and financing road maintenance. 

Mandates the use of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to evaluate road conditions in Monongalia and Preston Counties.

Requires the Commissioner of Highways to promulgate rules for legislative approval concerning data collection and road assessment.

Instructs the Division of Highways employees to drive all roads in the pilot counties for data capture.

Utilizes GPS, geotagged positioning, and laser measuring systems to assess road geometry and conditions.

Employs video documentation and reflectometer systems for comprehensive road condition analysis.

Requires biannual data capture and processing over three years to track road condition changes and provide predictive maintenance analysis.

name: Massachusetts H 4885 (Firearm Laws), Section 148
summary:
Establishes a special legislative commission to study emerging firearm technology, including personalized and microstamp technologies.

Requires the commission to evaluate the risks associated with using digital firearm manufacturing codes for machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Mandates the investigation of the accuracy, effectiveness, and utility of personalized firearm and microstamp technologies.

Instructs the commission to review any legal or constitutional issues relating to these technologies.

Tasks the commission with evaluating the commercial availability of these technologies for new and existing firearms.

Directs the commission to assess the feasibility and utility of a tax incentive program for personalized firearm technology.

Obliges the commission to submit its study and recommendations, including legislative suggestions, by March 1, 2025.

name: Connecticut H 5524 (General Government And School Building Projects), Sec. 143-144
summary:
Administers an artificial intelligence education tool pilot program by the Department of Education for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025.

Awards a grant by the Commissioner of Education for implementing an AI tool in classrooms, involving five selected school districts.

Requires the inclusion of at least one rural, suburban, and urban district, reflecting state diversity.

Mandates compliance of the AI tool with laws on AI use and student data privacy, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.

Defines "artificial intelligence" as technology using data to train algorithms for tasks usually associated with human intelligence.

Provides professional development for educators in the pilot program, covering AI tool utilization and privacy laws.

Trains educators on AI benefits for instruction, student learning, academic achievement, and workforce development.

name: Utah HB 148 (Artificial Pornographic Images Amendments)
summary:
Amends definitions related to child and vulnerable adult sexual abuse material, including depictions created or modified using computer-generated images.

Defines "distribute" and "produce" in the context of such materials, emphasizing the inclusion of electronic and computer-generated methods.

Criminalizes the distribution of intimate images without consent, outlining penalties, including misdemeanors and felonies for repeat offenses.

Exempts certain entities like law enforcement, legal proceedings, and internet service providers from liability if they incidentally transmit or store such images without intentional engagement.

Addresses sexual extortion, detailing offenses involving coercion through threats to distribute intimate images, with enhanced penalties for aggravated offenses involving children or vulnerable adults.

Prohibits unlawful distribution of counterfeit intimate images, specifying penalties and exemptions for certain entities and situations.

Specifies that the act takes effect on May 1, 2024, providing ample time for stakeholders to comply with the new regulations.

name: Illinois HB 2123 (Digital Forgeries Act)
summary:
Amends the Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act to define terms such as "depicted individual," "consent," and "dissemination."

Establishes a cause of action for depicted individuals against those who intentionally disseminate or threaten to disseminate private sexual images without consent, knowing or disregarding the individual's lack of consent and identifiability.

Clarifies that consent to creation or previous disclosure of an image does not imply consent to further dissemination.

Specifies exceptions to liability, including good faith actions by law enforcement, legal proceedings, and medical contexts, and outlines conditions under which parents or guardians are not liable.

Allows prevailing plaintiffs to recover damages, attorney's fees, and seek injunctive relief, while considering factors like age and dissemination scope.

States that disclosure of digitally altered images is not a defense and does not impose liability on interactive computer services for third-party content.

name: Mississippi SB 2577 (Wrongful Dissemination of Digitizations)
summary:
Establishes criminal penalties for wrongful dissemination of deepfakes, defined as realistic digital alterations of images or audio using AI or other technologies, particularly if used to influence elections.

Criminalizes dissemination within 90 days of an election without consent and with intent to harm a candidate or election outcome.

Imposes penalties of up to five years imprisonment or $10,000 fines for violations intended to incite violence or deter voting, with lesser penalties for other cases.

Allows injunctive relief actions by various parties, including the Attorney General and affected candidates, to prevent violations and remove disseminated deepfakes.

Exempts certain broadcasters and publishers, including those involved in bona fide news reporting or satire, from liability.

Requires clear labeling of deepfakes as a defense to prosecution.

Takes effect on July 1, 2024.

name: Indiana HB 1047 (Sexual Offenses)
summary:
Amends Indiana law to define "computer generated image" as images created or modified through artificial intelligence or software.

Prohibits distribution of intimate images without consent, including AI-generated images, categorizing such distribution as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenders.

Criminalizes voyeurism involving AI or cameras, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenses or distribution of recorded images.

Establishes that using unmanned aerial vehicles to capture private images without consent constitutes remote aerial voyeurism, punishable as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenses or distribution.

Exempts certain distributions of images for criminal investigations or under court orders.

Requires commencement of actions for child sexual abuse before certain deadlines or conditions, with exceptions for specific bankruptcy proceedings.

Declares an emergency for the enactment of these provisions.

name: Washington HB 1999 (Fabricated Sexually Explicit Images)
summary:
Amends Washington state law to address the creation, possession, and dissemination of fabricated intimate or sexually explicit images using digitization, including artificial intelligence.

Defines "fabricated depiction" as images altered to show minors or adults engaging in sexual conduct that did not occur.

Criminalizes disclosing fabricated intimate images without consent, establishing it as a gross misdemeanor or a class C felony for repeat offenders.

Specifies exemptions for disclosures made in the public interest, such as legal, law enforcement, or medical contexts.

Clarifies that interactive computer services and telecommunications providers are not liable for third-party content.

Establishes civil remedies for victims of unauthorized disclosures, including economic, noneconomic, and punitive damages.

Mandates that fabricated depictions remain in law enforcement custody and are not duplicated during legal proceedings.

Specifies timelines for filing civil actions related to unauthorized disclosures, especially for minors.

name: Illinois SB 382 (Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Sexual Images)
summary:
Amends the Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act to include "digitally altered sexual image" as a defined term, expanding the scope of protection to cover images that are substantially altered to falsely appear authentic.

Specifies that exceptions to liability apply to both private sexual images and digitally altered sexual images, maintaining exceptions for good faith actions by law enforcement, legal proceedings, medical education, and reports of unlawful or unwelcome conduct.

Clarifies that the dissemination of a private or digitally altered sexual image is not a matter of public concern solely because it involves a public figure or is accompanied by a political message.

Retains provisions that a parent or guardian is not liable for dissemination unless done for prohibited purposes, such as sexual gratification or commercial gain. 

Establishes that the Act takes effect upon becoming law, without acceleration or delay from previous or other legislative changes.

name: Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good (IDAIS)
summary:
Recognizes AI safety as a global public good, urging global governance to mitigate risks from advanced AI systems.

Encourages states and AI developers to commit to foundational principles for responsible AI development, fostering cooperation at intergovernmental summits.

Calls for states to establish and resource AI Safety Institutes to advance testing, research, and standards-setting.

Urges development of domestic authorities to detect and respond to AI incidents, coordinating globally for contingency planning.

Proposes Emergency Preparedness Agreements and Institutions for model registration, incident reporting, and contingency plans.

Establishes a Safety Assurance Framework requiring developers to demonstrate AI safety before deployment.

Calls for post-deployment monitoring and independent audits to ensure AI systems' safety.

Calls for independent global AI safety and verification research, funded by a diverse range of stakeholders.

Encourages international collaboration to develop verification methods, enabling credible safety claims and fostering trust.

name: Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence (IDAIS)
summary:
Proposes red lines in AI development and governance development as an international coordination mechanism to prevent catastrophic risks.

Prohibits AI systems from self-replication or improvement without human approval.

Restricts AI from taking actions to increase its power or influence unduly.

Forbids AI systems from aiding in the development of weapons of mass destruction.

Prohibits AI from autonomously executing cyberattacks causing significant harm.

Prevents AI from deceiving designers or regulators about its capabilities.

Calls for comprehensive governance regimes to prevent crossing of red lines.

Requires domestic registration of advanced AI models for government oversight.

Conditions global market access on compliance with internationally aligned regulations.

Encourages multilateral institutions to govern AGI development safely.

Mandates developers demonstrate adherence to red lines through evaluations and proofs.

Urges international collaboration on AI safety research and funding. 

Emphasizes decisive action combining technical research and governance to mitigate risks.

name: IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023)
summary:
Encourages governments worldwide to develop measures to prevent worst-case AI outcomes from malicious or careless actors and manage AI safety risks.

Recommends mandatory registration for creating, selling, or using AI models above a certain capability threshold to enhance government visibility into emerging risks.

Encourages governments to implement requirements to monitor large-scale data centers, track AI incidents, and mandate independent third-party audits for AI developers concerning information security and model safety.

Proposes defining clear red lines that, if crossed, mandate immediate termination of an AI system through rapid and safe shut-down procedures.

Urges international cooperation to establish and maintain the capacity to shut down AI systems crossing red lines.

Calls for AI developers to demonstrate to regulators that their systems will not cross defined red lines before deployment.

Advocates for substantial research progress to ensure advanced AI alignment with designers' intent and robustness against malicious actors.

Encourages a global network of AI safety research and governance institutions, with leading developers committing significant resources to AI safety.
